astra-6.text:
I think the useful way to think about it is that sequence and structure are coupled. You’re not just choosing a string of amino acids and then asking what it folds into. You’re trying to choose the atoms and their arrangement together, in the context of whatever you want the protein to interact with.

An all-atom representation lets you express that interaction at the level where it actually happens. The backbone matters, but so do the side chains—their geometry, how they pack, and which chemical groups face the target. Those details are part of the design problem.

Conceptually, diffusion gives you a way to turn an initially noisy candidate into a coherent molecular structure, conditioned on the target and the constraints you care about. The important distinction is that producing a plausible structure isn’t the same as producing a successful design. You still have to test whether it binds, whether it’s specific, and whether it behaves the way you intended.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to frame it is that you’re designing a three-dimensional interaction, not just a sequence. The sequence matters because it determines the chemistry, but what you ultimately care about is how those atoms arrange themselves relative to a target.

In an all-atom diffusion formulation, you can represent the target and the molecule you’re designing in the same geometric space. You condition on the parts you know, leave the designable parts free, and learn to generate arrangements that are compatible with that context. The challenge is coupling those geometric choices to chemical identity: you need something that both makes the interaction you want and corresponds to a protein that can actually adopt that structure.

That’s the appeal of the representation to me. It lets you pose design as generating a molecular complex under constraints, with sequence and structure as closely connected parts of the problem.
